Arbelos Bui

GeometryCirclesArea
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: three half-circles make a shoemaker's knife, with two new circles tucked inside.
How to play: Drag A, B or C along the bottom line, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, equal lengths or a hint.
Look for the math

Move the middle point and the two small circles change size. Yet the two new circles always have the same radius, their centres always sit the same distance from the middle of the big circle, and two tiny chords always add up to one diameter. Here is why.

The shoemaker's knife

An arbelos is the shape left inside the big semicircle on AB when the two smaller semicircles on AC and CB are cut away. Write r1 = AC/2 and r2 = CB/2. The big semicircle then has radius R = r1 + r2. Drag C to see the two halves trade size while their sum stays put.

The newly born circles

Above the midpoint of AC, the big semicircle meets the perpendicular bisector of AC at D₁. The lines D₁A and D₁C cut the small semicircle again at E₁ and F₁. Symmetry makes E₁F₁ parallel to AC. The page's proportion E₁F₁ / AC = BC / AB gives E₁F₁ = 2·r1·r2/(r1+r2), so the circle whose diameter is E₁F₁ has radius r = r1·r2/(r1+r2). That is exactly the radius of Archimedes' twins. The same argument on the other side gives K₂ the very same radius. The check tried 2,160 positions; both radii matched the formula every time to within a millionth.

Why the centres are equally far from O

Let O be the midpoint of AB, the centre of the big circle. The Pythagorean theorem in the triangle with corners O, O₁ and K₁ gives K₁O² = R² − r1·r2·(2r1+r2)(r1+2r2)/R². Swap r1 and r2 and you get K₂O², the same number. So K₁O = K₂O, the page's second claim, and the check found it true at every position too.

The extra chords and the area

Extend E₁D₁ and F₁D₁ until they meet the new circle again at G₁ and H₁, and do the same on the right. Those little chords have lengths 2r²/r1 and 2r²/r2, so G₁H₁ + G₂H₂ = 2r, as Bùi Quang Tuấn found. The related area article adds that the arbelos has area π·r1·r2 and each twin circle has area π·r²; both are checked here too.

A note on the source

The cut-the-knot article cited below now shows a GeoGebra sketch, so the Java applet's bytecode was used for the construction. In the applet A and B can be dragged off the baseline; here all three points stay on one line, so the picture is always a true arbelos. The applet also finds "the other intersection" with a one-unit distance test, which mistakes the endpoint for the far point when a semicircle is only a few units wide; this page takes the farther point, the same choice in every ordinary picture.

Try dragging C to the middle: the twins grow as large as they can, with radius R/4.
